stats.label: Frick objects on Wikidata (CC0), 197 of them paintings
Frick texts usable without a deal

findings.title: The Frick's own text needs a deal.
findings.body: frick.org says its content is for personal, educational, non-commercial use only. The Frick also publishes no open collection data (no CC0 dataset or API). Room texts, object essays, the audio guide and curator videos are all outreach. That makes the Frick target #1.

findings.title: Catalog facts come from Wikidata instead.
findings.body: Wikidata lists 209 Frick objects with accession numbers, artists and dates (CC0). That covers the paintings well but almost none of the decorative arts: porcelain, enamels, clocks, furniture and medals.

findings.title: Wikipedia covers the famous paintings.
findings.body: 43 objects have English articles, including the three Vermeers, both Holbeins, The Polish Rider, Bellini's Saint Francis and the Ingres. The rest of the paintings need library context plus Wikidata facts.

findings.title: There is useful public-domain material about Frick himself.
findings.body: The 1908 catalogue of Henry C. Frick's paintings (digitized by the Frick's own library) and George Harvey's 1928 biography are public domain. Both are period sources: the catalogue predates the museum, and the biography is admiring. The 1892 Homestead Strike needs balanced framing from Wikipedia.

findings.title: Most of the work is shared libraries.
findings.body: The Frick's strength is European painting and decorative arts by school. About 20 topic libraries (Dutch Golden Age, Venetian painting, French Rococo, British portraiture and others) would cover the rooms. The Met's European Paintings and decorative arts departments can reuse them.

sources.name: Wikidata
sources.gives: 209 Frick objects: accession numbers, artists, dates, materials, links to Wikipedia. Little decorative arts.

sources.name: Catalogue of the Henry C. Frick Collection of Paintings (1908)
sources.gives: Frick's own catalogue of his paintings before the museum. A companion 1908 exhibition catalogue also exists.

sources.name: George Harvey, Henry Clay Frick: The Man (1928)
sources.gives: Period biography. Admiring in tone, so tag it historical and pair it with Wikipedia on Homestead.

sources.name: Vasari, Lives of the Artists (de Vere translation, 1912–15)
sources.gives: Period lives of Bellini, Piero, Titian, Verrocchio, Pollaiuolo, Cimabue, Filippo Lippi, Gentile da Fabriano.

sources.name: Hofstede de Groot, Catalogue Raisonné of Dutch Painters (1908–1927)
sources.gives: Period scholarship on Vermeer, Hals, Cuyp, Hobbema, Ruisdael. Entries may name Frick's paintings and their earlier owners.

sources.name: Wikipedia (English)
sources.gives: 43 Frick objects, Frick history articles, and every library topic.

sources.name: Wikipedia (Spanish)
sources.gives: 20 Frick objects. Optional: the guide answers in the visitor's language from English sources.

sources.name: Getty vocabularies (AAT, ULAN)
sources.gives: Short artist bios (ULAN) and definitions for decorative-arts terms: famille noire, faience, marquetry, gilt bronze.

sources.name: Art Institute of Chicago API
sources.gives: Curatorial descriptions of comparable works (Rococo, Barbizon, Impressionism, Dutch) for library context.

sources.name: The Frick Collection: website, collection online, audio guide, videos
sources.license: © Frick; personal, educational, non-commercial use only
sources.gives: Room texts, object essays, the audio guide and curator videos. The best content for this venue.

sources.name: Smarthistory
sources.gives: Essays on several Frick works (Bellini, Holbein, Vermeer, Fragonard) and on most library topics.

sources.name: Essential Vermeer
sources.gives: Deep coverage of each Vermeer, including the Frick's three.

sources.name: Web Gallery of Art
sources.gives: Short commentaries on many Frick paintings.

sources.name: Frick Digital Collections (library)
sources.license: Per item: In Copyright / No U.S. Copyright / Not evaluated
sources.gives: Digitized archival material and books. Items marked No U.S. Copyright may be usable.

sources.name: RKD (Netherlands Institute for Art History)
sources.gives: Authoritative records for the Dutch and Flemish paintings.

sources.name: Library of Congress
sources.gives: Period photographs and texts for Gilded Age New York.

rate_limits.policy: One request at a time, at most 1 per second. Action API calls send maxlag=5. On 429 or 503, wait for Retry-After, otherwise back off exponentially (2s, 4s, 8s… up to 5 minutes). First check up to 50 titles' current revision IDs per call, then fetch only pages whose revision changed. User-Agent: ResearchBot/0.1 (leonardalonsostudio@gmail.com).
One query at a time, at least 2 seconds apart. Keep each query small (one per venue), because the service limits total query time per minute. Cache results.
At most 1 request per second. Download each book's full text once (the _djvu.txt file) and cache it. Never re-download unchanged items.
Stay under its published anonymous limit (60 requests per minute): 1 request per second.
Use the bulk downloads, not per-term requests.
Download from a mirror once and cache. Never crawl gutenberg.org pages.

Raw responses go into a local cache (gitignored .tmp/source-cache/, keyed by URL and revision), so re-running the puller repeats no network calls. Runs are resumable: a rate-limited run stops cleanly and the next run continues from the cache.
